title: Why You Keep Paying for a 'Free' Game (It's Not Bad Luck)

spine.goal: Dave downloads a free dragon game for his bus ride and wants to spend exactly $0 on it (his rule: never pay a cent).
spine.stakes: In three weeks the game takes $234.95 from him (five 'small' purchases); at that pace it is about $4,000 a year - money he never felt leave.
spine.central_question: How does a 'free' game get Dave to pay $235 without him ever feeling like he paid - and who is taking it?
spine.loop_big: Promised in o6: the REAL dollar price of the legendary dragon Dave was chasing, which the game hid behind gems. Paid in the last minute: up to about $356 (180 pulls x ~$2), while the banner only ever said '160 gems'.
spine.loop_mid: Pause-and-guess (~30%, end of ch2): on a normal day, out of every 100 people playing games like this, how many pay anything? Paid at the villain reveal: about 4 (Playtika FY2025 10-K: 370K daily payers / 8.5M daily players = 4.4%).
spine.villain: The game publisher's money design (with the app store taking its cut): built so ~96 in 100 play free while it hunts the few 'whales' - top 5% of loot box spenders = half of loot box revenue (Close et al., Addictive Behaviors 2021). Revealed ~50%.
spine.low_point: ~75%: 2 AM, Dave taps the second $99.99 pack (the flash-forward), pull 85 finally gives a legendary - the WRONG one (lost the coin flip). The dragon is 'guaranteed' only within 90 more pulls. Damage: $234.95, zero dragons.
spine.win: Dave fights back (education, not advice): adds up his purchase history ($234.95 as one number), builds a speed bump (Screen Time blocks in-app purchases / Google Play verification on every purchase, deletes saved card), uses the dollar rule + a $20 gift card a month. Meter flips to SAVED ~$3,800/yr. Final: converts the dragon to dollars - up to $356.

sources: Sensor Tower, 'State of Gaming 2026' report / press release (2026): mobile game in-app purchase (IAP) revenue reached about $82 billion worldwide in 2025 (~$81.75B)

U.S. Federal Trade Commission press release, Jan 17, 2025, 'Genshin Impact Game Developer Will be Banned from Selling Lootboxes to Teens Under 16 without Parental Consent, Pay a $20 Million Fine to Settle FTC Charges' (Cognosphere / HoYoverse): FTC alleged the game deceived players about the odds of winning 'five-star' loot box prizes and how much it would cost; players convert real money into virtual currency through multiple tiers with 'exchange rates in unusual denominations'; 'some children have spent hundreds or even thousands of dollars to win them'; order requires odds and real-money exchange-rate disclosures and an option to buy loot boxes directly with U.S. dollars

Genshin Impact in-game published wish details (Character Event Wish): 5-star base probability 0.600%; a 5-star is guaranteed within a maximum of 90 wishes; 50% chance a 5-star is the featured character, and if not, the next 5-star is guaranteed to be the featured one; one wish = 160 Primogems (Intertwined Fate). Store listing (Xbox / PlayStation stores): 6,480 Genesis Crystals for $99.99, +1,600 bonus crystals on repeat purchases (8,080 total), Genesis Crystals convert 1:1 to Primogems

Illustrative math for Dave's fictional dragon game (uses the same published rules as above): 8,080 gems per $99.99 -> 160 gems per pull = $99.99 x 160 / 8,080 = ~$1.98 (about $2) per pull; worst case 90 pulls + lost 50/50 + 90 more = 180 pulls x $1.98 = ~$356, before any free gems earned by playing. Odds 0.6% = about 1 in 167

Dave's purchases are a dramatized, illustrative story: $4.99 + $19.99 + $9.99 + $99.99 + $99.99 = $234.95 in three weeks; pace $234.95 / 3 weeks x 52 = ~$4,072 a year; with a $20/month gift-card budget = $240/yr; difference ~$3,832 (~$3,800) a year

Playtika Holding Corp., Form 10-K / Q4 & full-year 2025 results (filed 2026, SEC): 2025 revenue $2,755.4 million; Average Daily Active Users 8.5 million; Average Daily Paying Users 370 thousand; Average Daily Payer Conversion 4.4% (3.8% in 2024) -> about 4 in every 100 daily players pay

Close, J., Spicer, S.G., Nicklin, L.L., Uther, M., Lloyd, J. & Lloyd, H. (2021), 'Secondary analysis of loot box data: Are high-spending whales wealthy gamers or problem gamblers?', Addictive Behaviors, vol. 117: data on 7,767 loot box purchasers; the top 5% of spenders (> $100/month) represent half of loot box revenue; no significant correlation between loot box spend and earnings (rho = 0.02); confirmed correlation with problem gambling (rho = 0.34); developers disproportionately profit from moderate and high-risk gamblers rather than high-earning customers

U.S. FTC, Epic Games (Fortnite) order, finalized March 2023: Epic to pay $245 million to refund consumers over 'dark patterns' / button designs that led to unwanted charges; FTC refund rounds: Dec 2024 - 629,344 payments totaling more than $72 million; June 2025 - 969,173 payments totaling more than $126 million (about $200 million to ~1.6 million players)

Apple, App Store Small Business Program page and standard terms (2026): standard App Store commission on in-app purchases in the U.S. is 30% (15% for developers earning under $1 million a year and for some subscriptions)

Apple Support article 102470, 'Use Screen Time to turn off in-app purchases on your iPhone or iPad': Settings > Screen Time > Content & Privacy Restrictions > iTunes & App Store Purchases > In-app Purchases > Don't Allow

Google Play Help, 'Require authentication for purchases' (answer 1626831): Purchase verification can be set to 'Always' - verification for every purchase through Google Play's billing system, including within apps
Apple App Store Review Guidelines 3.1.1 (since Dec 2017): apps offering loot boxes 'must disclose the odds of receiving each type of item to customers prior to purchase'

beats.text: Two A M. Dave is about to tap a ninety nine dollar button. In a free game.
Yep. That's Dave. Let's rewind.
Three weeks ago. A free dragon game, for the bus. Dave's rule: never pay a cent.
But people spent eighty two billion dollars inside mobile games last year.
So who's taking it? And how, without Dave noticing?
By the end, you'll see the dragon's real price. The game hid it.
Day one. Dave taps install. No card, no charge. Just a cute dragon game and twenty minutes on the bus.
It's great. Level one. Level five. Level ten. Free, free, free.
Then level twelve. A boss. Dave loses. Again. And again. His energy bar hits empty.
The screen gives him two choices. Wait four hours. Or refill now, for two hundred gems.
Dave checks his gems. One hundred ninety. Ten short. Ten! And the smallest pack of gems costs four ninety nine.
It's like a theme park with free entry, where the roller coaster stops halfway up the hill and asks for a dollar.
So Dave taps buy. Five bucks, whatever. But that tap just told the game the most valuable thing about him. He pays.
The next day, Dave opens the shop. And he notices something weird.
Nothing in the shop costs dollars. A dragon egg? Three hundred twenty gems. A speed boost? Fifty gems.
And gems only come in packs, with a big yellow sticker that says best value.
It's like landing in a foreign country with funny colorful money. Day one, you do the math. By day three, you just hand over the paper.
And it's not just Dave. In twenty twenty five, the F T C, America's consumer watchdog, fined the maker of Genshin Impact twenty million dollars.
It said the game's layers of virtual money, with exchange rates in unusual numbers, hid how much real money players spent.
Dave buys the best value pack. Nineteen ninety nine. Nothing costs exactly that many gems, so he ends up with leftovers.
Quick guess. On a normal day, out of every hundred people playing games like this, how many pay anything at all? Write your number in the comments.
Because that night, a new message popped up. Season three starts now.
It's a season pass. Nine ninety nine. One hundred rewards, over thirty days.
But you don't get the rewards when you pay. You earn them by playing. Every single day.
Miss a few days, and the season ends before the good stuff. Then a brand new pass goes on sale.
It's like paying ten dollars for a chore chart. Fun, until you're doing chores at midnight so you don't lose your stickers.
So Dave buys it. Now he opens the game at eleven fifty eight P M, just to tap claim.
But the pass was just the warm up. That Friday, Dave met a glowing egg.
A banner explodes across Dave's screen. Legendary fire dragon. Forty eight hours only.
You can't buy the dragon. You buy pulls. Each pull cracks open an egg with a random prize.
The small print: chance of a legendary on each pull, zero point six percent. About one in a hundred sixty seven.
Like a cereal where one box in a hundred sixty seven has a gold toy. Every box costs two dollars. And the cereal is air.
The game promises a legendary by pull ninety. Ninety sounds far. But the timer is ticking.
So Dave buys the big pack. Ninety nine ninety nine. Fifty pulls. Rainbow lights. Drum rolls. Common sword. Common shield. Common potato.
Sixty pulls in, no dragon. Dave feels like the unluckiest player alive. But he isn't unlucky. He's exactly who this game was built for.
So Dave went looking for who actually pays for these free games.
He found the yearly report of Playtika, a big mobile game company that shares its numbers with U S regulators.
Remember your guess? On an average day in twenty twenty five, about eight and a half million people played its games. Three hundred seventy thousand paid.
That's about four out of every hundred. Ninety six play free. Four pay the bills. And the bills came to two point seven billion dollars.
Like a restaurant where ninety six people eat free, and four pay for everything. The waiter isn't watching the free eaters. He's watching who orders dessert.
The biggest spenders have a name in the industry. Whales. A study in the journal Addictive Behaviors looked at almost eight thousand loot box buyers.
The top five percent of spenders, paying over a hundred dollars a month, brought in half of all the loot box money.
That's the villain. A money machine built to find the few people who will pay a lot, and keep them paying. And on iPhones in the U S, Apple's standard cut is thirty percent.
Dave figured whales were rich guys with yachts. He was about to find out how wrong that was.
Dave thought whales were millionaires. Nope.
The same study checked if big spenders earned more money. They didn't. No link between spending and income.
What did go up with spending? Signs of problem gambling. These games profit most from people at risk, not from the rich.
And sometimes the whale is a kid. The F T C said some children spent hundreds, even thousands of dollars chasing Genshin's five star prizes.
And Fortnite's maker, Epic Games, had to pay two hundred forty five million dollars after the F T C said its buttons tricked players into purchases.
But Dave didn't feel tricked. He felt close. Which is how he ended up here. Two A M. Thumb over the ninety nine dollar button.
Tap. Fifty more pulls. Pull eighty five. Gold light! A legendary! A legendary knight. Not the dragon.
The fine print: a coin flip decides if your legendary is the one on the banner. Dave lost. The dragon is now guaranteed. Within ninety more pulls.
Two hundred thirty five dollars. Three weeks. Zero dragons. And for the first time, Dave put the phone down.
The next morning, Dave did three things. This is education, not advice.
One. He added up his purchase history. Five charges. Two hundred thirty four dollars and ninety five cents. As one number, it hurt more than the knight.
Two. A speed bump. On iPhone, Screen Time can switch off in app purchases. On Android, Google Play can ask for verification on every purchase. And he deleted his saved card.
Three. The dollar rule. Before buying, he turns gems back into dollars. And his game budget is one twenty dollar gift card a month.
At his old pace, that's about four thousand dollars a year. With the gift card, two hundred forty. Dave keeps about three thousand eight hundred.
But one question still bugged him. What did that dragon actually cost?
So Dave used the dollar rule on the dragon itself.
His game uses the same rules Genshin Impact publishes. Zero point six percent. A legendary by pull ninety. And the coin flip.
Each pull costs one hundred sixty gems. A ninety nine dollar pack gives about eight thousand gems. So every pull is about two dollars.
Worst case, you reach pull ninety, lose the coin flip, and need ninety more. One hundred eighty pulls.
One hundred eighty pulls, at about two dollars each. The dragon's real price? Up to three hundred fifty six dollars, before a few free gems.
The banner said one hundred sixty gems. It never said three hundred fifty six dollars. That's not an accident. That's the business.
Dave wasn't playing the game. The game was playing Dave. And it kept score in his bank account.
One. Gems are dollars in a costume. Take the costume off.
Two. About four in a hundred players pay for everyone. The game is hunting them.
Three. Build the speed bump before two A M, not during.
Next time, Dave's friend Bob is getting divorced. The lawyer says it'll be quick and simple. Then the first bill arrives.
Subscribe. It's free. Actually free. No gems, no eggs, no coin flips. We checked.
